Until the ownership requirement is met, the individual must retain at least 75% of net shares received from equity awards (after shares withheld for taxes). Shares counted toward the requirement include directly owned shares, shares held in retirement plans, unvested RSUs (at 50% value), and shares held by immediate family members in the same household.

items.question: What is the process for the board to approve a related-party transaction involving a 10% shareholder under the company's governance framework?
items.ground_truth: Under the Related Party Transaction Policy, any transaction involving a 10% or greater shareholder that exceeds $250,000 in value must be reviewed and approved by both the Audit Committee and the full board of directors (excluding any interested directors). The shareholder must disclose all material terms of the proposed transaction in writing. The Audit Committee must obtain an independent fairness opinion if the transaction value exceeds $5 million. The board must determine that the transaction is fair to the company and on terms no less favorable than arm's-length terms. The transaction and the board's determination must be disclosed in the company's annual proxy statement.

items.question: What is the definition of 'Disability' under the executive Employment Agreement and what benefits are triggered?
items.ground_truth: Section 5.4 defines 'Disability' as the executive's inability to perform the essential functions of their position, with or without reasonable accommodation, for a period of 180 consecutive days or 270 days in any 12-month period, as certified by a physician mutually agreed upon by the company and the executive. Upon termination due to Disability, the executive is entitled to: (a) accrued but unpaid base salary and bonus through the termination date; (b) continued payment of base salary for 12 months; (c) any vested benefits under the company's long-term disability plan; (d) continued vesting of equity awards for 12 months post-termination; and (e) 18 months of COBRA continuation at the company's expense.

items.question: What are the confidentiality obligations that survive termination of the employment relationship under the Employment Agreement?
items.ground_truth: Section 9.1 imposes a perpetual confidentiality obligation on the employee with respect to trade secrets, and a five-year post-termination obligation for all other confidential information. Confidential information is broadly defined to include business plans, customer lists, pricing data, financial information, product roadmaps, personnel information, and proprietary technology. The employee must return all company materials and delete all electronic copies upon termination. The surviving confidentiality obligation is independent of and in addition to any obligations under the separately executed Non-Disclosure Agreement. The provision is enforceable regardless of the reason for termination, whether voluntary, involuntary, for cause, or without cause.

items.question: What benefits are provided under the company's Employee Stock Purchase Plan (ESPP) and what are the enrollment terms?
items.ground_truth: The ESPP, qualified under Section 423 of the Internal Revenue Code, allows eligible employees (those with at least 90 days of service and working 20+ hours per week) to purchase company stock at a 15% discount to the lower of the fair market value on the offering date or the purchase date. Each offering period is six months, beginning on January 1 and July 1. Employees may contribute between 1% and 15% of eligible compensation through payroll deductions, subject to the IRS annual limit of $25,000 in fair market value of stock per calendar year. Enrollment occurs during designated enrollment windows (December 1–15 and June 1–15). Employees may withdraw from an offering period at any time, and accumulated contributions are refunded without interest.

items.question: What are the employer's obligations under the FMLA for an employee requesting intermittent leave for a chronic health condition?
items.ground_truth: Under the Family and Medical Leave Act, an eligible employee (12+ months of service and 1,250+ hours worked in the preceding 12 months at a covered employer with 50+ employees) is entitled to up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave per 12-month period for a serious health condition. Intermittent leave is permitted when medically necessary for a chronic condition that requires periodic treatment. The employer may require a medical certification from the employee's health care provider and may request recertification every 30 days. The employer must maintain the employee's group health insurance on the same terms during FMLA leave. Upon return, the employee must be restored to the same or an equivalent position with equivalent pay, benefits, and working conditions.

items.question: What are the employer's obligations when implementing a reduction in force under the Severance Plan?
items.ground_truth: The company's Severance Plan provides that in the event of a reduction in force (RIF), affected employees are entitled to: (a) base severance of two weeks' pay per year of service, with a minimum of four weeks and a maximum of 26 weeks; (b) a prorated annual bonus based on actual company performance; (c) continuation of health benefits at active employee rates for the severance period; (d) outplacement services for up to 90 days; and (e) accelerated vesting of any equity awards that would have vested within 90 days of termination. Payment is conditioned on execution of a separation agreement including a general release of claims. The company must comply with WARN Act notification requirements and ensure that the selection criteria for the RIF do not have a disparate impact on any protected group.

items.question: What background check and drug testing provisions are included in the conditional offer of employment letter?
items.ground_truth: The conditional offer letter states that the offer is contingent upon satisfactory completion of: (a) a comprehensive background check including criminal history (7-year lookback), employment verification for the past 10 years, education verification, and professional license verification; (b) a pre-employment drug screening using a 10-panel urine test; and (c) verification of the candidate's right to work in the United States via I-9 documentation. The candidate must consent in writing to the background check in compliance with the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA), including receiving a summary of rights. If adverse action is taken based on the background check, the company must provide a pre-adverse action notice with a copy of the report and a 5-business-day waiting period before the final adverse action notice.

items.question: What is the scope of the copyright registration for the software application as described in the IP filing documentation?
items.ground_truth: The copyright registration filed with the U.S. Copyright Office covers the original literary work embodied in the software application's source code, user interface design elements, and accompanying documentation. The registration identifies the software company as the author under the work-made-for-hire doctrine and claims the date of first publication as March 15, 2024. The deposit material consists of the first and last 25 pages of source code with trade secret redactions permitted under 37 C.F.R. § 202.20(c)(2)(vii). Copyright registration establishes prima facie evidence of the validity of the copyright and the facts stated in the certificate, and is a prerequisite to filing a copyright infringement suit for works of U.S. origin under 17 U.S.C. § 411.

items.question: What obligations does the licensee have regarding quality control under the Trademark License Agreement?
items.ground_truth: Section 5.1 of the Trademark License Agreement requires the licensee to maintain the quality of goods and services offered under the licensed marks at a level consistent with or superior to the quality standards specified in the Brand Standards Manual (Exhibit D). The licensee must submit samples of all products and marketing materials bearing the marks to the licensor for approval at least 30 days before first commercial use. The licensor has the right to inspect the licensee's facilities and operations upon reasonable notice to verify quality compliance. Failure to maintain quality standards constitutes a material breach entitling the licensor to terminate after a 30-day cure period. Quality control is essential to prevent the licensed marks from becoming generic or losing distinctiveness, which could constitute a 'naked license' rendering the marks unenforceable.

items.question: What are the patent prosecution and maintenance obligations under the Exclusive License Agreement?
items.ground_truth: Section 4.2 obligates the licensor to prosecute and maintain all patents in the licensed portfolio at its own expense, including filing continuation and divisional applications where commercially reasonable. The licensor must provide the licensee with copies of all material patent office communications and allow the licensee to review and comment on responses before filing. If the licensor decides to abandon any licensed patent, it must give the licensee 60 days' written notice, and the licensee may assume prosecution at its own expense while retaining the license. The licensor must pay all maintenance fees when due and provide the licensee with evidence of timely payment. Failure to maintain a patent due to the licensor's negligence entitles the licensee to a proportional reduction in royalties and damages for any lost patent protection.

items.question: How does the most-favored-licensee clause in the Patent License Agreement protect the licensee's competitive position?
items.ground_truth: Section 3.8 provides that if the licensor grants a license to any third party under the same patents on terms more favorable than those in the licensee's agreement (including lower royalty rates, broader field of use, or fewer restrictions), the licensee is automatically entitled to the same more favorable terms retroactive to the date they were first granted to the third party. The licensor must notify the licensee within 30 days of granting any new license and provide a summary of the material commercial terms (redacted for the third party's confidential information). The licensee has 60 days to elect whether to adopt the more favorable terms. This provision does not apply to settlement licenses entered into to resolve bona fide patent infringement litigation.

items.question: What are the data portability and interoperability requirements in the SaaS Subscription Agreement's IP provisions?
items.ground_truth: Section 8.4 provides that the customer retains all ownership rights in its data uploaded to or generated by the SaaS platform ('Customer Data'). The vendor grants no license rights in Customer Data except as necessary to provide the services. Upon termination or expiration of the subscription, the vendor must make all Customer Data available for export in a standard, machine-readable format (CSV, JSON, or XML) for a period of 90 days post-termination at no additional charge. After the 90-day period, the vendor will delete all Customer Data from its systems and provide written certification of deletion. The vendor must support standard API-based data export throughout the subscription term and may not use data lock-in tactics to impede the customer's ability to migrate to an alternative platform.

items.question: Under the Trade Secret Protection Agreement, what constitutes unauthorized disclosure and what are the immediate remedies?
items.ground_truth: Section 2.3 defines unauthorized disclosure as any communication, transmission, publication, or making available of protected trade secret information to any person not authorized under the agreement, whether intentional, negligent, or through failure to implement required security measures. Section 6.1 provides that upon discovery of an unauthorized disclosure, the disclosing party must immediately notify the trade secret owner within 24 hours, take all reasonable steps to prevent further dissemination, cooperate in identifying the scope of the disclosure, and preserve all evidence related to the breach. The trade secret owner may seek emergency injunctive relief without bond and may invoke the expedited arbitration procedure in Section 12 for damages, which must be initiated within 30 days of discovery.

items.question: What are the fair use considerations when the licensee uses excerpts of the licensed content for commentary and criticism?
items.ground_truth: The Content License Agreement in Section 6.2 acknowledges that the licensee's use of brief excerpts of the licensed content for purposes of commentary, criticism, news reporting, or scholarship may constitute fair use under 17 U.S.C. § 107, which is not restricted by the agreement. The fair use analysis considers four factors: (1) the purpose and character of the use, including whether it is commercial or transformative; (2) the nature of the copyrighted work; (3) the amount and substantiality of the portion used in relation to the whole; and (4) the effect of the use on the potential market for the original work. The agreement specifies that excerpts of up to 300 words from any single work, when accompanied by proper attribution, are deemed within the scope of fair use for the purposes of the agreement.

items.question: What is the standard for compelling a third-party witness to testify at a deposition in a federal civil action?
items.ground_truth: Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 45, a party may compel a non-party witness to attend a deposition by serving a subpoena. The subpoena must be issued from the court in the district where the deposition is to be taken and may command the witness to appear at a location within 100 miles of the witness's residence, place of employment, or regular place of business. The serving party must tender the witness fee ($40 per day) and mileage at the prescribed rate. The witness may move to quash or modify the subpoena if it creates undue burden, requires disclosure of privileged material, or fails to allow reasonable time to comply. A non-party may also be compelled to produce documents at the deposition under Rule 45(a)(1)(A)(iii).

items.question: What are the requirements for filing a motion to compel discovery under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37?
items.ground_truth: Under Rule 37(a), a party seeking to compel discovery responses must first make a good-faith effort to confer with the opposing party to resolve the dispute without court intervention, as required by the meet-and-confer obligation. If the dispute remains unresolved, the moving party files a motion to compel with the court, specifying the discovery requests at issue, the deficiencies in the responses, and the relevance of the requested information. The motion must include a certification that the movant made the required good-faith effort to resolve the dispute. If the motion is granted, Rule 37(a)(5) provides that the court must order the non-compliant party to pay the movant's reasonable expenses, including attorneys' fees, unless the non-compliance was substantially justified or other circumstances make the award unjust.

items.question: What is the standard for granting a motion for summary judgment under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 56?
items.ground_truth: Under Rule 56(a), a court shall grant summary judgment if the movant shows that there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. The movant bears the initial burden of demonstrating the absence of a genuine issue of material fact, either by affirmative evidence or by pointing to the absence of evidence supporting the non-movant's claim. Once the movant meets this burden, the non-movant must go beyond the pleadings and designate specific facts showing a genuine issue for trial, supported by affidavits, depositions, or other admissible evidence. The court views the evidence in the light most favorable to the non-movant and draws all reasonable inferences in the non-movant's favor. Mere conclusory allegations or denials are insufficient to defeat summary judgment.

items.question: What procedures govern the appointment and challenge of arbitrators under the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules?
items.ground_truth: Under the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules (2021 revision), Articles 7–12 govern arbitrator appointments. For a three-member tribunal, each party appoints one arbitrator within 30 days of a request, and the two party-appointed arbitrators appoint the presiding arbitrator within 30 days of their appointment. If any appointment is not made within the time limit, the appointing authority (designated by the parties or by the Permanent Court of Arbitration at The Hague) makes the appointment. A party may challenge an arbitrator within 15 days of learning of circumstances giving rise to justifiable doubts as to the arbitrator's impartiality or independence. If the other party does not agree to the challenge, the appointing authority decides the challenge. The IBA Guidelines on Conflicts of Interest provide an influential framework for evaluating challenges.

items.question: What are the requirements for enforcing a foreign arbitral award under the New York Convention in U.S. federal court?
items.ground_truth: Under the Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards (New York Convention), as implemented by Chapter 2 of the Federal Arbitration Act (9 U.S.C. §§ 201–208), a party seeking to enforce a foreign arbitral award must file a petition to confirm the award in a U.S. district court within three years of the award. The petitioner must supply the authenticated original award or a certified copy and the original arbitration agreement or a certified copy. The respondent may oppose confirmation only on the limited grounds set forth in Article V of the Convention, including invalidity of the arbitration agreement, lack of due process, excess of arbitral authority, improper tribunal composition, and public policy. U.S. courts apply a strong presumption in favor of confirmation, and the burden is on the party resisting enforcement.

items.question: What is the procedure for initiating an inter partes review of a patent before the USPTO Patent Trial and Appeal Board?
items.ground_truth: Under 35 U.S.C. §§ 311–319, any person who is not the patent owner may file a petition for inter partes review (IPR) with the PTAB challenging the validity of one or more claims of an issued patent on grounds of anticipation or obviousness based on prior art patents or printed publications. The petition must be filed within one year of the petitioner being served with a patent infringement complaint. The petition must identify each claim challenged, the prior art relied upon, and the specific grounds for unpatentability with particularity. The PTAB decides whether to institute the IPR within six months of filing, applying a 'reasonable likelihood' standard. If instituted, the PTAB must issue a final written decision within 12 months (extendable by six months for good cause). The petitioner bears the burden of proving unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence.

items.question: What are the landlord's obligations for maintaining the building's structural components under the Commercial Lease?
items.ground_truth: Section 9.1 of the Commercial Lease assigns responsibility for structural maintenance exclusively to the landlord. Structural components include the roof, exterior walls, foundation, load-bearing walls, structural columns, and the building's structural frame. The landlord must maintain these components in good condition and in compliance with all applicable building codes throughout the lease term. The landlord is responsible for the cost of structural repairs and capital replacements, though capital expenditures may be amortized over their useful life and partially passed through to tenants as operating expenses to the extent they benefit the tenant's premises. The landlord must respond to emergency structural issues within 24 hours and complete non-emergency structural repairs within a commercially reasonable timeframe not to exceed 30 days.

items.question: What insurance requirements does the tenant need to satisfy under the Triple Net (NNN) Lease?
items.ground_truth: Section 10.1 of the NNN Lease requires the tenant to maintain: (a) commercial general liability insurance with limits of $3 million per occurrence and $5 million in the aggregate; (b) property insurance covering the tenant's improvements and personal property at full replacement cost; (c) business interruption insurance covering at least 12 months of rent; (d) workers' compensation at statutory limits; and (e) umbrella/excess liability coverage of $5 million. The landlord and its mortgage lender must be named as additional insureds on the CGL policy and as loss payees on the property insurance policy. All policies must be issued by carriers rated A- or better by A.M. Best and must provide 30 days' advance written notice of cancellation or material modification. Certificates of insurance must be delivered annually and upon each policy renewal.

items.question: What are the tenant's rights under the Right of First Refusal clause for adjacent space in the Office Lease?
items.ground_truth: Section 24.1 grants the tenant a right of first refusal (ROFR) on any contiguous space on the same floor that becomes available during the lease term. When the landlord receives a bona fide third-party offer for the ROFR space, the landlord must notify the tenant in writing, providing the material terms of the offer including the proposed rent, term, tenant improvement allowance, and free rent concessions. The tenant has 10 business days to elect to lease the ROFR space on the same terms. If the tenant declines or fails to respond within the 10-day period, the landlord may lease the space to the third party on terms no more favorable than those offered to the tenant. If the landlord does not execute a lease with the third party within 180 days, the ROFR reattaches to the space.

items.question: What are the percentage rent provisions in the Retail Lease for a restaurant tenant in a mixed-use development?
items.ground_truth: Section 4.3 of the Retail Lease requires the restaurant tenant to pay percentage rent equal to 6% of gross sales exceeding the natural breakpoint (defined as base rent divided by the percentage rent rate). With a base rent of $180,000 per year and a percentage rate of 6%, the natural breakpoint is $3,000,000 in annual gross sales. Gross sales include all revenue from food and beverage sales, catering, delivery, and gift card redemptions, but exclude sales tax collected, employee meals, complimentary items, and refunds. The tenant must submit monthly gross sales reports within 15 days of each month-end and an annual certified statement within 90 days of year-end. The landlord has the right to audit the tenant's sales records once per year.

items.question: What signage rights are granted to the office tenant in the multi-tenant building lease?
items.ground_truth: Section 23.1 grants the tenant the right to install building-standard suite identification signage adjacent to the entrance of the premises and listing on the building's lobby directory, at the landlord's expense. If the tenant leases at least one full floor (10,000+ RSF), the tenant is entitled to floor lobby identification signage at the tenant's expense, subject to the landlord's design approval. Tenants leasing 25,000 RSF or more are entitled to monument signage at the building entrance and one panel of exterior building signage, subject to municipal approval and the landlord's sign criteria in Exhibit F. All signage must comply with applicable zoning ordinances and the building's architectural standards. Upon lease expiration, the tenant must remove its signage and restore the affected areas to their original condition.

items.question: What are the anti-bribery compliance requirements in the Third-Party Agent Due Diligence Policy?
items.ground_truth: The Third-Party Agent Due Diligence Policy requires that before engaging any agent, distributor, or intermediary who will interact with government officials on the company's behalf, the compliance department must conduct risk-based due diligence including: (a) verification of the agent's identity, business registration, and beneficial ownership; (b) screening against global sanctions lists, enforcement databases, and politically exposed person (PEP) lists; (c) review of the agent's anti-corruption compliance program; and (d) reference checks with at least two prior principals. The engagement agreement must include anti-corruption representations and warranties, audit rights, and a right to terminate immediately if the agent violates any anti-bribery law. For agents operating in high-risk jurisdictions (as defined by the Transparency International CPI), enhanced due diligence and senior management approval are required.

items.question: What are the basic reporting requirements for a Form 8-K filing with the SEC following a material definitive agreement?
items.ground_truth: Under SEC rules, a public company must file a Form 8-K within four business days of entering into a material definitive agreement not made in the ordinary course of business (Item 1.01). The filing must include a brief description of the material terms and conditions of the agreement, including the parties, the date of execution, and any material relationships between the registrant and the other parties. The company must file the actual agreement as an exhibit to the 8-K, subject to the ability to request confidential treatment for commercially sensitive terms under Rule 24b-2. Failure to timely file a Form 8-K may result in SEC enforcement action and loss of eligibility to use short-form registration statements (Form S-3) for capital-raising transactions.

items.question: What are the minimum requirements for a company's written information security program under the FTC Safeguards Rule?
items.ground_truth: The FTC Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 314), as amended in 2023, requires financial institutions to develop, implement, and maintain a comprehensive written information security program. Key requirements include: (a) designating a qualified individual (CISO or equivalent) to oversee the program; (b) conducting a written risk assessment identifying reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks; (c) implementing safeguards including access controls, encryption of customer information in transit and at rest, multi-factor authentication, and secure development practices; (d) regularly testing and monitoring the effectiveness of safeguards through penetration testing (annually) and vulnerability assessments (every six months); (e) providing security awareness training to all employees; (f) overseeing service providers' security practices; and (g) establishing a written incident response plan. The qualified individual must report in writing to the board or governing body at least annually.

items.question: What are the record-keeping requirements under the HIPAA Privacy Rule for a covered entity?
items.ground_truth: Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule (45 C.F.R. Part 164, Subpart E), covered entities must maintain required documentation for a minimum of six years from the date of creation or the date when the policy was last in effect, whichever is later. Required records include: (a) the entity's privacy policies and procedures; (b) privacy practices notices; (c) authorizations for uses and disclosures of protected health information (PHI); (d) records of complaints received and their disposition; (e) business associate agreements; (f) an accounting of disclosures made for purposes other than treatment, payment, and health care operations; and (g) documentation of workforce training. The covered entity must designate a privacy officer responsible for developing and implementing the privacy program and must have a process for individuals to file complaints about privacy practices.

items.question: What are the key provisions of the company's Code of Conduct regarding gifts and entertainment from third parties?
items.ground_truth: Section 7 of the Code of Conduct permits employees to accept gifts and entertainment from third parties only if they are: (a) of nominal value (not exceeding $150 per item or $500 in the aggregate per year from any single source); (b) not in the form of cash or cash equivalents; (c) given in the ordinary course of business and not in connection with any pending decision or transaction; and (d) consistent with customary business practices in the industry. Gifts exceeding the thresholds must be reported to the compliance department within five business days and may be accepted only with prior written approval from the employee's supervisor and the Chief Compliance Officer. Gifts from government officials or in connection with government contracts are subject to additional restrictions under applicable procurement integrity rules.

items.question: What are the annual compliance training requirements under the company's regulatory compliance program?
items.ground_truth: The Compliance Program requires all employees to complete annual training modules covering: (a) anti-corruption and anti-bribery (FCPA and UK Bribery Act); (b) antitrust and fair competition; (c) insider trading and securities compliance; (d) data privacy and cybersecurity (GDPR, CCPA, and sector-specific requirements); (e) export controls and trade sanctions; and (f) workplace harassment and discrimination prevention. New employees must complete all modules within 30 days of hire. Employees in high-risk roles (sales, procurement, government affairs, and finance) must complete enhanced modules specific to their function. Training completion is tracked through the company's learning management system, and managers receive quarterly reports on team completion rates. Employees who fail to complete required training within the deadline are subject to progressive disciplinary action, and their supervisors' compliance metrics are impacted.

items.question: What are the regulatory approval requirements for a bank merger under the Bank Merger Act?
items.ground_truth: The Bank Merger Act (12 U.S.C. § 1828(c)) requires that any merger involving FDIC-insured depository institutions receive prior approval from the responsible federal banking agency (the OCC for national banks, the Federal Reserve for state member banks, and the FDIC for state nonmember banks). The application must include detailed information on the financial condition of both institutions, the terms of the merger, the impact on competition, and the convenience and needs of the communities served. The agency must consider the competitive effects of the merger (in consultation with the DOJ), the financial and managerial resources of the resulting institution, the convenience and needs of the community, and the effectiveness of the parties' anti-money laundering programs. The agency must publish notice of the application and provide a 30-day public comment period. The DOJ has an additional 15-day post-approval window to challenge the merger on antitrust grounds.

items.question: What are the Dodd-Frank whistleblower provisions and how do they incentivize reporting of securities violations?
items.ground_truth: Section 922 of the Dodd-Frank Act (15 U.S.C. § 78u-6) established the SEC Whistleblower Program, which provides monetary awards to individuals who voluntarily provide original information to the SEC that leads to successful enforcement actions resulting in sanctions exceeding $1 million. The award amount ranges from 10% to 30% of the total monetary sanctions collected. The SEC considers factors including the significance of the information, the degree of assistance provided, the SEC's programmatic interest in deterring violations, and whether the whistleblower participated in internal compliance systems. The Act prohibits retaliation by employers against whistleblowers, providing a private right of action with remedies including reinstatement, double back pay, and attorneys' fees. Whistleblower submissions may be made anonymously through an attorney.

items.question: What is the structure of the escrow holdback for the working capital adjustment in the Asset Purchase Agreement?
items.ground_truth: Section 2.7 of the Asset Purchase Agreement provides that $2 million of the closing consideration is deposited into an escrow account with Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. as escrow agent, solely to secure the post-closing working capital adjustment. The escrow amount is held for 120 days following closing to allow time for the final determination of the net working capital. Once the working capital adjustment is finalized (either by agreement of the parties or determination by the Accounting Arbitrator), the escrow agent distributes the appropriate amount to the buyer or seller, and any remaining balance is released to the seller. The escrow is invested in U.S. Treasury money market instruments, with interest following the principal. The escrow agreement contains standard provisions for disputed claims, successor escrow agents, and indemnification of the escrow agent.

items.question: What are the employee benefit plan continuation obligations of the buyer following the closing of the stock acquisition?
items.ground_truth: Section 6.4 of the Stock Purchase Agreement requires the buyer to maintain, for at least 12 months following closing, employee benefit plans that provide compensation and benefits (including base salary, annual bonus opportunity, health and welfare benefits, and retirement benefits) that are, in the aggregate, substantially comparable to those provided by TargetCo immediately before closing. The buyer must recognize employees' prior service with TargetCo for purposes of eligibility and vesting under the buyer's benefit plans. The buyer must waive pre-existing condition exclusions and waiting periods under its health plans to the extent waived under TargetCo's prior plans. Accrued but unused vacation and paid time off must be honored by the buyer. These obligations do not require the buyer to maintain any specific plan or prevent the buyer from terminating any employee for cause.

items.question: What is the break-up (termination) fee payable by the target company if it terminates the Merger Agreement to accept a superior proposal?
items.ground_truth: Section 8.3(b) provides that if TargetCo's board terminates the Merger Agreement to enter into a definitive agreement with respect to a Superior Proposal (as defined in Section 1.1), TargetCo must pay AcquirerCo a termination fee of $18 million (representing approximately 4% of the equity value of the transaction) in cash by wire transfer within two business days of such termination. The termination fee is also payable if TargetCo's board withdraws or adversely modifies its recommendation and AcquirerCo subsequently terminates. The parties agreed that the termination fee represents a reasonable estimate of costs and damages incurred by AcquirerCo and is not a penalty. Receipt of the termination fee is AcquirerCo's sole and exclusive remedy against TargetCo for termination under these circumstances, except in cases of intentional or willful breach of the Merger Agreement.

items.question: What representations does the buyer make regarding its financing commitment in the Merger Agreement?
items.ground_truth: Section 4.5 requires the buyer to represent and warrant that: (a) it has received executed commitment letters from its financing sources providing for aggregate debt financing sufficient, together with available cash and equity commitments, to fund the full merger consideration, repay existing target indebtedness, and pay all transaction expenses; (b) the commitment letters are in full force and effect and have not been amended or waived; (c) no event has occurred that would permit the financing sources to terminate the commitments or fail to fund; (d) the buyer has fully paid all commitment fees and other amounts due under the commitment letters; and (e) the buyer is not aware of any fact or circumstance that would reasonably be expected to prevent the financing from being obtained on the terms described in the commitment letters. The buyer covenants to use its reasonable best efforts to obtain the financing on the terms set forth in the commitment letters.

items.question: What post-closing purchase price adjustments are available to the parties under the Membership Interest Purchase Agreement?
items.ground_truth: Section 2.5 provides for three post-closing adjustments: (a) a net working capital adjustment comparing the final closing net working capital to the target of $8.2 million, with dollar-for-dollar adjustments above or below the target; (b) a net debt adjustment for the difference between estimated and actual closing-date indebtedness (including all funded debt, capital lease obligations, accrued interest, and deferred purchase price obligations); and (c) a cash adjustment for any excess cash on the balance sheet above a minimum cash threshold of $500,000. The buyer prepares the closing statement within 75 days post-closing. The seller has 30 days to review and object. Any true-up payment (in either direction) is due within five business days of the final determination and accrues interest at the prime rate from the closing date.

items.question: What is the term of the exclusive license grant and what happens to the license upon expiration?
items.ground_truth: Section 2.3 of the Exclusive License Agreement grants the licensee an exclusive license for an initial term of seven years from the effective date, with an automatic renewal for successive two-year periods unless either party provides 12 months' written notice of non-renewal. Upon expiration or termination, the licensee must cease all use of the licensed patents and return or destroy all confidential technical documentation within 30 days. The licensee retains a non-exclusive, paid-up license to sell off existing inventory of licensed products manufactured before the termination date for a period of 180 days following expiration. Any sublicenses granted during the term survive expiration to the extent they were properly authorized and the sublicensee remains in compliance.

items.question: What is the geographic scope of the non-disclosure agreement between the two joint venture partners?
items.ground_truth: Section 1.2 of the NDA provides that the confidentiality obligations apply worldwide, without geographic limitation, reflecting the global nature of the joint venture's operations. The NDA covers all confidential information exchanged in connection with the proposed joint venture, including business plans, financial data, customer information, technical specifications, and trade secrets. The term of the NDA is three years from the effective date for general confidential information, and trade secrets remain protected for as long as they retain trade secret status under applicable law. The NDA is governed by New York law, and disputes are resolved by arbitration in New York under AAA Commercial Arbitration Rules.

items.question: What are the permitted uses of the licensed software under the End User License Agreement for enterprise deployment?
items.ground_truth: Section 2.1 of the EULA grants the enterprise licensee a non-exclusive, non-transferable right to install and use the software on up to 500 named-user seats within the licensee's organization for internal business purposes only. The license prohibits use by third parties, affiliates not listed in the order form, or contractors who are not under the licensee's direct supervision. The licensee may make one backup copy for archival purposes. The license does not permit redistribution, sublicensing, hosting the software for third-party access (SaaS), or using the software to provide services to third parties (service bureau use). The licensee may use the software across multiple physical locations provided the total named-user count does not exceed the licensed quantity.

items.question: What are the requirements for the landlord to provide an estoppel certificate to the tenant's prospective lender?
items.ground_truth: Section 21.1 requires that within 15 business days of a written request from the tenant, the landlord must execute and deliver an estoppel certificate confirming: (a) the lease is in full force and effect and has not been modified (or stating the modifications); (b) the commencement and expiration dates; (c) the current base rent and additional rent; (d) the amount of any security deposit held; (e) whether either party is in default (and if so, specifying the nature of the default); and (f) that no rent has been paid more than 30 days in advance. The estoppel certificate may be relied upon by the tenant's lender, assignee, or subtenant. Failure by the landlord to deliver the certificate within the required period is deemed a confirmation that the statements in the tenant's proposed form are correct.

items.question: What are the basic disclosure obligations in a Schedule 13D filing when an investor acquires more than 5% of a public company's stock?
items.ground_truth: Under Section 13(d) of the Securities Exchange Act and Rule 13d-1, any person who acquires beneficial ownership of more than 5% of a class of equity securities registered under Section 12 must file a Schedule 13D with the SEC within 10 calendar days of crossing the 5% threshold. The filing must disclose: (a) the identity and background of the reporting person; (b) the source and amount of funds used to acquire the securities; (c) the purpose of the acquisition (including any plans for mergers, acquisitions, or other extraordinary transactions); (d) the number of shares beneficially owned and the percentage of the class; and (e) any contracts, arrangements, or understandings with respect to the securities. Material changes in the information must be reported via an amendment promptly. Passive investors may file the shorter Schedule 13G if they certify the securities were acquired in the ordinary course of business without the purpose of changing or influencing control.
